item.content:encoded:

All proposed edits will be in a collapsible below this post, and after 7 days if there are no serious objections to the edits, the feedback received will be taken into account as the edits are made. If you have questions not directly related to the article about this project, please pm a member of the WikiWalk Team

Seeing has how both SCP-259 and SCP-508 serve as windows to other places when viewed, its not so far out of line for Johnny Foundation to investigate a potential connection between the two phenomena. As such, I am recommending the following edits:

Changing this:

Foundation mathematicians are working on determining why this specific fractal has anomalous properties, and whether other similarly anomalous images exist. By O5 order, any image rendering related to SCP-259 experimentation must take place at least ████ m from inhabited areas.

To this:

Foundation mathematicians are working on determining why this specific fractal has anomalous properties, and whether other similarly anomalous images exist. By O5 order, any image rendering related to SCP-259 experimentation must take place at least ████ m from inhabited areas.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

I figured I might as well explain my edit in more detail here.
This might be a nitpick, but that's not how a portal to the vacuum of space would work. It would cause all the air in the location to rush into the portal but only at enough speed to pick up light debris. In the event that the portal would be opened in a closed room, a break would be created in either a door or a window by the extreme vacuum, but it in no way would be with sufficient force to implode an entire building. Now, if the portal was to open up near a black hole or on a neutron star… then you would definitely get the effects described.

item.content:encoded:
I guess that's just a matter then of the Containment procedures being overall all over the place and a mess, in some cases up to subjective decision. Still, I feel even by the site's old guide on containments, this one in particular doesn't suit a Keter classification.

Containing SCP-259 is as easy as putting the disc in a sleeve and putting it in a locked box under your bed. Meanwhile, something like SCP-106 requires constantly reinforced walls, and an entire area filled with cells filled with random trash, and lots of lights focused on the entire room 24 hours a day without interruption. Instances of 259 popping up randomly can be tracked down and contained. There's likely to be casualties leading up to its discovery, but there's no real risk of the same instance breaking out again.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Already brought up and answered back in July.

But the basis of the criticism is a misconception. A fractal is not necessarily infinite, it's just that they can be extrapolated infinitly. Take the Serpinski triangle, the simplest fractal I'm aware of. Start with an equalateral triangle, now join the mid-points of the three sides to create another, inverted, equalateral triangle inside the first. Stop. What you have drawn is a fractal. You can repeat the steps, making half-again as tall triangles forever. But that first shape-inside-a-shape is still, technically, a fractal figure.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I have to call BS on this- You can't "render" a fractal image, in the literal sense.

It's infinite regression, represented on a finite space (finite specially, finite pixels, finite dots-per-inch, finite subatomic particles to assume the pattern) whatever measure you care to use, to render the entirety of a fractal image is mechanically impossible.

I upvoted anyway, because my mathematical nitpicking is a silly reason to rag on an otherwise really cool page.

And, you could totally incorporate this feature of fractals into the SCP, levels of detail changing some property of the effect like portal size etc?

item.content:encoded:
if this pattern opens a portal that usually has stuff that kills people, then how do they know what it vaguely looks like?

Since SCP-259 is computer generated, it's possible to tweak the parameters in the generating program to produce something that is close to the SCP image, but does not have anomalous effects. It's dangerous to try, because you won't know that it won't do anything until you generate it.

Also, a dimension filled with spiders has been done before, see SCP-507.

Giant spiders are pretty iconic in horror fiction. Would you like giant cockroaches better?

We already got SCP-508

OK, we do. SCP-508 is:

— an autostereogram, which means its effect is entirely based on a trick of human perception
— non-reproducible, according to the author
— not very dangerous. The effects are mostly benign/whimsical. The only reason the thing is dangerous is that the scientists didn't let the D-Class leave the room or stop looking at 508 when they saw something disturbing.

I think it's a superficial similarity, and the feel of the article is totally different.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm assuming (it's late here, and I'm falling asleep) that you're saying: "Wait, you can't 100% completely render a fractal image because they're infinitely self-similar." — and you're right. All of the fractal images we see are actually approximations, and when I said "completed rendering" in the SCP, I meant that the computer finished rendering the image to the level of detail it was programmed to. In-universe, that should be close enough to produce the anomalous effect.

Out-of-character, one of the things I learned while writing this is that for a mathematical SCP to work, it has to make sense to all the non-mathematicians (without them having to go look stuff up, or feeling like they are being taught math instead of reading a story). At the same time, it has to not sound like complete BS to the folks who know more about the underlying math. It's a fine line and I've probably leaned towards staying away from any overly mathematical details.
